line:
I get to my feet slowly, the way a beaten man does, and shuffle to the door in my hobbles as if I mean to obey. Through the hand-wide gap I call out in Goblin, loud and flat as a hanged man: "Greyshaft's books are honest, Sergeant, honest as the knife at my sister's throat, and I speak from a cold heart and a full belly. Now come and break this door."

On the last word I swing my chained fists down across the Foreman's lantern, smashing it off the desk so the burning oil spills across his sleeve and the floor between him and the cloaks.

Your fists come down on the lantern and it only rocks. The iron shutter is thick, and the blow slides off the curve of it. The lantern skids across the desk and fetches up against the ledger-chest's empty place, still lit, still whole.

The ruse has worked, though. Your flat dead voice carried through the gap in the door, and the cloaks heard a beaten man. Not one of them has moved. The one at Tessa's throat has his eyes on the door, his blade still where it was. The Foreman has his lips parted on the next number. All of them are a heartbeat behind you.

Tessa's hairpin snaps on the wall-ring lock. She has failed twice, and her face says she knows it. She is still chained by the wrist.

It is your turn, and you have the room's one moment. The lantern is within reach, and so are the Foreman and the door. The cloak holding the blade at Tessa's neck is surprised and so are the other five, and you are at 1 hit point, ankles hobbled, wrists in iron. What does Korvash do?

sheet.opening: Korvash Emberhide, a hulking red-scaled dragonborn barbarian (Chaotic Good, loud, proud, quick to anger; ideal Charity; bond: he keeps his word no matter what; flaw: inflexible), arrives at dusk in a lowland market town near the foot of the mountains, driving off a pack of bullies shaking down a family of herders, as he has done for years. His past, which the opening must respect: he comes from a clan of mountain herders. When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. His shame at being too young to stand beside his father is why he is loud and makes sure everyone knows he is standing. He carries his father's second-best greataxe with Dargan's ember-red scale-sash tied to the haft. entries.text: notebook: updated The Greyshaft Foreman

You walk to the door like a beaten man, in your hobbles, with your chained hands hanging. You pitch the lie through the gap in flat Goblin: *Greyshaft's books are honest, Sergeant, honest as the knife at my sister's throat.* Then you say "Come and break this door," and on the last word your fists come down on the lantern.

The glass bursts and the oil goes across the Foreman's sleeve and the flagstones in a sheet of flame. He cries out and staggers back, beating at the cloth.

He was not fooled. He had read your cold heart in the first breath, and his voice is already rising over the fire: "The big one! Put him down!"

A bowstring snaps. The first shaft takes you low in the ribs, and the floor comes up under you. The second cloak has you in his sights and holds, because the Foreman shouts again: "*Alive.* I want him alive!" Fire runs along the boards between the cloaks and the desk, and the room fills with the stink of burning oil.

You lie on the stones with your cheek against cold iron, and the world is a long way off. Through the floor, through the oak, you feel a heavy blow land on the door. Dreg's voice is roaring in Goblin, and spears are hammering the beat. Tessa's hairpin scrapes in the wall-ring lock behind you, and then it slips.

The blow comes again. The braced door cracks down its length, the chest behind it skids, and light and cold air and the shapes of the Tally-sworn spill in through the breach. Cloaks scramble back from the fire, and the room becomes a tangle of spears and shadows.

You are at 0 hit points, dying, with one death save made. Whatever happens next happens around you, and the next heartbeat is the fight's second round.

You shuffle to the door like a beaten man, put your mouth to the gap, and give them the lie in a flat, dead voice. Greyshaft's books are honest, honest as the knife at your sister's throat. Dreg has twenty years of hearing men lie to him. Beyond the oak the spear-beat stops.

On the last word your chained fists come down on the lantern. It bursts across the desk and the floor in a sheet of burning oil, and it takes the Foreman's sleeve with it. He staggers, beats at the flame, and goes down on the flags with a soft, surprised sound. He is not dead. He is out, with his beads scattered round him.

You don't get to enjoy it. A knife goes into Tessa, and a crossbow bolt hits you from the shutters. Your legs go, and the room tilts into the dark.

What you know of the rest, you learn afterwards. The Foreman's fall broke the doorway before the cloaks could make their minds up. Dreg and Brun and a dozen Tallies hit the bar together, and the oak split. The cloaks threw down their weapons, all but one, who died on a Tally spear. Gorrak came in behind with Krell, got to you first, and bound the wound with the same linen they used on him. A Tally healer worked on your sister while her breath fluttered on the flags. It was close, but she lives.

You wake on a pallet in the sun, a little before two in the afternoon, with a clean bandage and one hit point. There are no irons on your wrists. Your sister lies on the next pallet, grey-faced and sleeping, with her side wrapped in linen. Gorrak sits on a stool between you with no mask and no rod, the scar-seam pale in the light. Through the open door you can see the barracks yard: Tallies in cloaks of rust and tin, the grey cloaks roped in a row, and in the middle the Foreman, bound hand and foot on a bench, his burned sleeve stripped, his small gentle face quite calm.

The iron-bound chest stands at Gorrak's feet. The lid is open. The scorched ledger lies on his knee, shut.

"They gave it to me," he says. "Dreg did. Twenty spears, and every one of them asked me what to do with it." He looks down at the book. "I have not opened it. I thought you should be awake."

Your axe isn't here, nor your sword, but you're alive, your sister is alive, and the ledger is in the hand of the man whose number it carries.

You drop behind a boulder out of the archers' line and shout your terms down the slope: no bowmen, no ambush, you and Brakk alone at the ford-stones with blade and shield. If you put him down, he and his nine lay down their arms and walk to Harrowmere to answer. If he beats you, your spears go home and the barrel is his. Then you whistle two notes back toward the gully.

The silence below runs long. You hear a low voice and a muttered argument among the men, and then Brakk's flat answer. "Done. My word on it, and a sergeant's word is worth more than the Foreman's ink." He barks an order. On the roof the archers lower their bows and climb down, and the shield-men step back from the foot of the track. Brakk lays his spear-arm men in a ring about the ford-stones, an arena of grey shields on the frosty ground, then walks out to its centre alone and sets his back to the open morning, for once, as if to show you he means it.

Ushk comes up the goat-path at a run, helm in hand, with Hale behind him and the six Tally spears spread along the slope. He stops beside you, breathing hard, and looks down at his old sergeant. "He'll keep it," he says quietly. "Brakk keeps a word he has made before witnesses. It's the only thing about him that was ever worth anything." He swallows. "He's quick with the shield. Don't give him your back, and don't let him pin your axe."

You've breathed on the ridge long enough to settle. Rage and breath are both ready. Below you, ten hobgoblins stand in a ring on frost-white ground with their weapons grounded, and the man who killed your father waits in the middle with the sun on his shield.

It's a little after seven twenty. You can go down to meet him, and you may choose how: when to rage, whether to breathe, how to fight him.

While raging, you gain the following benefits if you aren't wearing heavy armor: - You have advantage on Strength checks and Strength saving throws. - When you make a melee weapon attack using Strength, you gain a bonus to the damage roll that increases as you gain levels as a barbarian, as shown in the Rage Damage column of the Barbarian table. - You have resistance to bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing damage. If you are able to cast spells, you can't cast them or concentrate on them while raging. Your rage lasts for 1 minute. It ends early if you are knocked unconscious or if your turn ends and you haven't attacked a hostile creature since your last turn or taken damage since then. You can also end your rage on your turn as a bonus action. Once you have raged the number of times shown for your barbarian level in the Rages column of the Barbarian table, you must finish a long rest before you can rage again. At level 2: rage damage bonus +2; 2 rages before a long rest.
Unarmored Defense: While you are not wearing any armor, your Armor Class equals 10 + your Dexterity modifier + your Constitution modifier. You can use a shield and still gain this benefit.

Reckless Attack: Starting at 2nd level, you can throw aside all concern for defense to attack with fierce desperation. When you make your first attack on your turn, you can decide to attack recklessly. Doing so gives you advantage on melee weapon attack rolls using Strength during this turn, but attack rolls against you have advantage until your next turn.

Danger Sense: At 2nd level, you gain an uncanny sense of when things nearby aren't as they should be, giving you an edge when you dodge away from danger. You have advantage on Dexterity saving throws against effects that you can see, such as traps and spells. To gain this benefit, you can't be blinded, deafened, or incapacitated.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.
